base_properties.human_readable: Magisterial Integralist Reading: Catholic Anthropology in AI Governance

stakeholders.name: catholic_magisterium
stakeholders.situation: The teaching authority of the Church claims unique standing to interpret human dignity through the imago Dei doctrine and to guide technological development through Catholic Social Doctrine. Sets normative frameworks for AI design that embed Catholic anthropology: person as relational, embodied, finite yet transcendent. Authority derives from lineage (apostolic succession, papal magisterium) and theological expertise. Enforcement is through moral suasion, institutional witness, and appeal to conscience of AI developers and policymakers.

stakeholders.name: vulnerable_populations
stakeholders.situation: Workers, the poor, migrants, the elderly, and those without technical literacy bear the extractive burdens of AI systems most acutely — algorithmic discrimination in hiring, surveillance in labor management, social isolation through automation, elder abandonment. The Magisterial reading protects their dignity as irreducible, requiring AI design to respect relational and embodied human goods. Their exit options are severely constrained; they depend on institutional advocacy and legal safeguards.

stakeholders.name: workers
stakeholders.situation: Face displacement through automation and algorithmic management systems that treat labor as a cost to be minimized rather than as participation in human dignity and community contribution. The Magisterial reading affirms the right to meaningful work, just wages, and dignity in labor — directly contradicting purely efficiency-driven AI development. Their advocacy capacity is higher than powerless populations but remains constrained by capital mobility and technical opacity.

stakeholders.name: families
stakeholders.situation: Experience erosion of familial bonds through surveillance technology, social media algorithms designed to maximize engagement over relational health, and economic pressures from AI-driven labor displacement. The Magisterial reading emphasizes the family as the foundational social unit and site of human flourishing; it requires AI governance to protect family stability and intergenerational transmission of values.

stakeholders.name: faith_communities
stakeholders.situation: Religious communities (Catholic parishes, dioceses, and international networks) benefit from the Magisterial reading's authority claim — they become central institutional voices in AI governance discourse. Catholic Social Teaching provides a framework for collective witness and advocacy. They have some exit options through ecumenical or secular alliances but derive much of their institutional standing from this particular theological claim.

stakeholders.name: transhumanist_projects
stakeholders.situation: Philosophical and technical movements aimed at transcending biological limits through AI and biotechnology face direct constraint from the Magisterial reading. Projects that treat the human body as a platform for enhancement, that aim at uploading consciousness, or that seek to obsolete biological humanity are declared contrary to Catholic anthropology. Their exit option is to argue against the Magisterial framework's legitimacy; they bear the cost of not being able to claim moral endorsement from Catholic institutions.

stakeholders.name: technocratic_elites
stakeholders.situation: Technology industry leadership, venture capital, and academic technologists who treat AI development as a domain best governed by expertise and market mechanisms rather than moral theology. The Magisterial reading constrains their autonomy by asserting that AI design must answer to questions of human dignity and the common good, not only to efficiency and innovation metrics. They have exit options through regulatory arbitrage (moving operations to jurisdictions with lighter moral constraint) and through counter-claims that technological progress is itself a form of human flourishing.

stakeholders.name: unregulated_ai_developers
stakeholders.situation: Developers and startups operating without institutional oversight or community accountability face the constraint most directly through pressure from Catholic institutions, ethical review expectations, and reputational cost. They bear the cost of slowed development timelines, design mandates that embed relational anthropology, and the need to justify extractive or transhumanist features. Many operate internationally and cannot easily exit Magisterial pressure where Catholic institutions or politically sympathetic jurisdictions shape policy.

stakeholders.name: secular_humanist_advocates
stakeholders.situation: Proponents of secular human-rights frameworks and democratic deliberation on AI governance would argue that privileging Magisterial authority undermines pluralism and concentrates governance power in a religious institution. They are structurally excluded from the agenda-setting role within this reading's framework. Their objection would center on the authority claim itself: that theological anthropology should not override democratic process.

stakeholders.name: techno_optimist_philosophers
stakeholders.situation: Advocates for technological enhancement and transcendence of biological limits are structurally excluded from recognition as legitimate voices in this reading's framework. The Magisterial reading treats their core project (technological transcendence) as inimical to human dignity rightly understood. They would argue this exclusion is imposed without their consent and represents a form of epistemic violence against their vision of human flourishing.

stakeholders.name: policymakers_in_catholic_majority_regions
stakeholders.situation: Government and regulatory authorities in countries with substantial Catholic populations (Latin America, much of Europe, Philippines) sit between the Magisterial claim to authority and secular legal orders. They must navigate the Magisterial reading's influence on public conscience while maintaining secular legitimacy and pluralist governance. Their observations shape whether the reading becomes enforceable law or remains moral suasion.

stakeholders.name: secular_policymakers_in_mixed_jurisdictions
stakeholders.situation: Regulatory authorities in secular or religiously plural democracies observe the Magisterial reading's claims but face legitimacy constraints if they embed one theological tradition into law. Their role is analytical: to assess whether the anthropological claims track public consensus, whether they serve the common good across multiple worldviews, and how to balance Magisterial witness with other moral frameworks.

six_questions.coordination_function: Solves the problem of how to design AI systems that embed respect for human dignity as irreducible, relational, and transcendent — rather than as instrumental efficiency or as a platform for posthuman enhancement. Provides a shared anthropological framework (imago Dei, Catholic Social Doctrine) that coordinates the values embedded in AI architecture, labor policy, family protection, and governance structures.
six_questions.transfer_function: Transfers agenda-setting authority over AI design from technological experts and market actors to the Magisterium and faith-aligned institutions. Moves compliance costs from corporations to developers (design constraints, ethical review, slowdown of innovation). Extracts recognition and institutional authority for Catholic teaching as a binding voice in technology governance.
six_questions.absent_voices: Secular humanists, techno-optimists, and proponents of democratic pluralism who would argue that no single theological tradition should have authority over AI governance. Transhumanist thinkers and enhancement advocates who view the Magisterial reading's anthropology as a constraint on human flourishing. Voices of technologically displaced workers from regions without Catholic institutional infrastructure. Engineers and developers in non-Catholic-majority jurisdictions who experience this reading's influence as imposed without their consent.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: If the Magisterial integralist reading vanished, AI development would accelerate toward efficiency-maximizing and enhancement-enabling designs; labor regulation would relax; family-protective design mandates would lift; governance authority would consolidate in secular technical and market institutions. Catholic institutions would lose their distinctive voice in technology ethics. Vulnerable populations would lose an organized institutional advocate rooted in dignity claims beyond utility. The anthropological grounding of AI design would shift from theological transcendence to secular capability maximization.
six_questions.founding_problem: Early AI development (2010s–2020s) operated under a technocratic, predominantly secular framework that treated AI as a neutral tool for whatever goals its builders chose. This framework systematized discrimination, displaced workers, eroded family bonds, and subordinated human dignity to efficiency metrics. Catholic moral theology observed that no technology is neutral; all embeds anthropological claims. The founding problem was: how can the Church's witness to human dignity as imago Dei shape AI development to protect vulnerable populations and preserve relational human goods?
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: The Magisterium attests the founding problem is live through Vatican documents (Fratelli Tutti, 2020; Caritas in Veritate on technology; papal addresses on AI). Independent verification comes from: labor economists documenting AI-driven displacement without social protection (Acemoglu & Johnson, MIT); family researchers documenting social-media effects on relational health (Boyd, Turkle, Dunn); bioethicists from secular traditions (Floridi, Vallor) corroborating that AI systems do embed anthropological claims. The founding problem status is contested only by techno-optimists and pure-efficiency advocates; independent observers from outside the benefiting parties (vulnerable populations, faith communities) attest that the technological-neutrality framework has failed to protect human dignity.

commentary.narrative_context: The Magisterial Integralist reading asserts that human dignity is an ontological gift from God (imago Dei), infinite and inalienable, knowable through faith and reason. It claims that AI governance must conform to Catholic Social Doctrine principles as interpreted by the Magisterium, and that the Church has unique authority to guide technological development toward the common good. This is ONE reading of the contested kernel 'human dignity in AI governance.' Other readings (secular-humanist, techno-optimist, pluralist-pragmatic) instantiate different constraints with different beneficiaries, extraction mechanisms, and authority claims. This story authorizes only the Magisterial reading as a clean, ε-invariant constraint. The sibling readings are separate constraint stories, not variations of this one.
key_agents: Catholic Magisterium (institutional agenda-setter, civilizational time horizon)
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness at 0.48 is moderate-to-substantial because the constraint demands structural transformation (AI design must embed Catholic anthropology) but relies on voluntary adoption through moral suasion rather than legal coercion in most jurisdictions. The constraint extracts from technocratic elites and transhumanist projects (who lose autonomy to prioritize efficiency and enhancement) and from unregulated developers (who face design mandates and ethical review burdens). It benefits vulnerable populations and workers by asserting their dignity as irreducible and requiring AI systems to protect relational and embodied human goods. Suppression is relatively low (0.35) because enforcement mechanisms are primarily institutional witness and moral appeal rather than coercive exclusion; developers can technically exit by operating in secular jurisdictions, though they bear reputational cost. Theater ratio is low (0.22): the Magisterial reading's functions (protecting dignity, coordinating anthropological grounding, advocating for vulnerable populations) are substantively real. The metric series show gradual rise from t0 to t25, reflecting slow institutional expansion of Catholic AI ethics initiatives and increasing pressure on tech companies to respond to Magisterial critique—extraction increases as the reading's influence hardens into policy expectations and ESG frameworks. Suppression requirement rises similarly as the reading must push back harder against technocratic inertia. Theater stays flat after t15, indicating the constraint's function remains stable (not degrading into pure performance).
commentary.perspectival_gap: The Magisterium and faith communities experience this constraint as genuine coordination of anthropological values; they are the designers and beneficiaries of the framework. Technocratic elites and transhumanist developers experience it as an imposed external constraint on their autonomy and research agendas. Vulnerable populations and workers experience it as advocacy and protection from a powerful institutional voice—but that protection depends on the Magisterium's willingness to maintain the anthropological claim and on political power to enforce design constraints. The engine should compute this divergence: from the Magisterial seat, the constraint is coordination-enabling; from the technocratic seat, it is extraction. From the vulnerable-population seat, it is protective alliance, but contingent on institutional continuity.
commentary.directionality_logic: Directionality ranges from d≈0.0 (vulnerable populations as full beneficiaries: the constraint subsidizes their dignity-protection) through d≈0.5 (faith communities as mostly beneficiaries but also invested in defending the arrangement) to d≈0.9 (transhumanist projects and unregulated developers as targets: the constraint extracts their autonomy). Technocratic elites sit near d≈0.85 (powerful, but their core project is constrained; they have arbitrage exit but bear reputational cost). The beneficiary-victim split is sharp: the constraint creates a clear coalition (vulnerable, workers, families, faith communities) and clear opposition (transhumanist, technocratic efficiency-maximizers). No directionality override is needed; the beneficiary/victim declarations cleanly map to the structural positions.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The founding problem (lack of dignity-respecting framework in early AI development) is LIVE and CONTESTED: the Magisterium attests it remains; independent observers (labor economists, family researchers, bioethicists) corroborate that efficiency-driven AI has failed to protect vulnerable populations. Techno-optimists contest whether dignity should constrain enhancement, but they do not deny the founding problem exists—they dispute its weight relative to innovation. This is not mandatrophy (function atrophied, persistence theatrical); it is healthy tangled rope. The constraint genuinely solves a coordination problem (embedding anthropological values in AI design) AND imposes asymmetric extraction (constraining technocratic autonomy). Both functions are live. Mandatrophy would manifest if the Magisterium ceased to actually advocate for vulnerable populations and instead used dignity-language as theatrical cover for institutional power—the theater_ratio is not high enough (0.22) to trigger that reading. The constraint's persistence depends on actual enforcement (Vatican documents, institutional pressure, reputational cost), not on institutional inertia alone.
commentary.kernel_context: This constraint instantiates the magisterial_integralist_reading of the contested kernel human_dignity_ai_governance. Sibling readings: secular_humanist_reading (dignity grounded in rational autonomy and UDHR, governance through democratic deliberation), techno_optimist_reading (dignity enhanced through technological augmentation, minimal restriction), pluralist_pragmatic_reading (dignity as contested across traditions, governance through overlapping consensus). The Magisterial reading's unique structure: authority grounds itself in theological lineage (apostolic succession, papal magisterium) and claims to integrate faith and reason into a transcendent anthropology. Sibling readings coexist as live positions in global discourse; none forecloses another within a single framework. The readings influence each other: Magisterial authority pressure shapes policymaking in Catholic-majority regions (structural influence on techno-optimist and secular-humanist constraints). This story is one constraint among four sibling constraints, each authored as clean ε-invariant stories with separate beneficiaries, extractiveness profiles, and authority claims.

omegas.question: Does the Magisterium's authority to guide AI governance depend on theological legitimacy (faith community acceptance, doctrinal coherence) or on institutional power (Catholic institutional density in a region, economic leverage of Catholic organizations)? Is the authority claim self-sustaining or contingent on non-theological factors?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Comparative analysis of Magisterial influence in regions with high and low Catholic institutional density; examination of whether Magisterial critiques of AI shape policy in secular jurisdictions; survey of whether policy adoption tracks theological conviction or institutional pressure.
omegas.impact: If authority is primarily theological, the constraint is sustainable long-term and reflects genuine conviction among beneficiaries. If authority is contingent on institutional power, the constraint is vulnerable to institutional decline or to institutional capture (the Magisterium prioritizing institutional interests over dignity protection). Classification does not change, but understanding of the constraint's persistence mechanism shifts.
omegas.description: Whether Magisterial authority grounds in theology or institutional power.

omegas.question: Is the extracted constraint (AI systems must embed Catholic anthropology) tightly coupled to the theological claim (human dignity as imago Dei), or can the policy demands be decoupled from their theological grounding and adopted on secular grounds (dignity as human rights, common-good governance)?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Empirical tracking of whether secular jurisdictions and non-Catholic technologists adopt the anthropological constraints while rejecting the theological foundation; whether the policy cluster (labor protection, family-protective design, vulnerability focus) remains coherent without the imago Dei grounding.
omegas.impact: If decoupling is possible, the constraint's longevity does not depend on theological legitimacy—a secular version could persist after faith commitment declines. If tightly coupled, the constraint is vulnerable if Magisterial authority itself declines. This does not change the constraint's type, but predicts its evolution under different conditions.
omegas.description: Whether the policy cluster can persist without its theological grounding.

omegas.question: Does the Magisterium's institutional protection of vulnerable populations depend on the Magisterium's benign intent and accurate discernment of vulnerable interests, or could institutional power concentrated in the Magisterium become a vector for controlling vulnerable populations' voices (paternalism masquerading as dignity protection)?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Examination of decision-making processes: are vulnerable populations (workers, the poor, migrants) at the table when Magisterial AI governance is formulated, or are they represented by clergy and institutional theologians? Historical analysis of whether Magisterial protection has tracked vulnerable-population agency or institutional convenience.
omegas.impact: If vulnerable populations are genuinely co-determining the constraint, the beneficiary classification is robust. If representation is merely nominal, the constraint risks reclassification: from beneficiary-protecting tangled rope to a snare where the Magisterium extracts authority by speaking FOR vulnerable populations without their voice. This is an omega about the authenticity of the beneficiary claim, not its structure.
omegas.description: Whether Magisterial protection of vulnerable populations reflects their own agency or institutional paternalism.

omegas.question: Can the Magisterial integralist reading be sustained without claiming unique authority for theological anthropology? If a pluralist pragmatic approach (overlapping consensus, procedural fairness across traditions) adopted all the policy outputs (labor protection, family-protective design, vulnerability focus) while explicitly denying the Magisterium's authority claim, would the constraint remain the same or become a different constraint?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Thought experiment: model a pluralist-pragmatic regime that enforces identical AI design mandates through secular human-rights and common-good language. Compare the extractiveness profiles, enforcement mechanisms, and beneficiary/victim positions. Assess whether the readings produce materially different constraints or merely different legitimation stories for the same rules.
omegas.impact: If the constraint is distinct from the pluralist reading, it must be because the Magisterial authority claim is structurally essential—not just a rhetorical wrapper. If the policies are separable from authority, then the 'constraint' is really the shared policy cluster, and the readings are alternative legitimations of it. This is a conceptual omega about whether we have one constraint with multiple readings or multiple constraints with overlapping outputs.
omegas.description: Whether the Magisterial reading's distinctness depends on its authority claim or only on its policy outputs.

omegas.question: Is the measured suppression (0.35) structural (institutional exclusion of non-Catholic voices, policy restrictions on code) or partly internalized (tech workers with secular worldviews who have internalized the constraint through ESG training, ethical AI certification, or career incentives)? After the constraint is removed, does suppression persist?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Post-exit analysis: survey technologists who have left regulated environments or faith-aligned institutions; assess whether constraint internalization persists. Track whether workers with secular commitments who adopt the constraint do so because they believe in it or because institutional pressure makes refusal costly.
omegas.impact: If suppression is largely structural, the constraint's power depends on institutional enforcement—it decays if enforcement relaxes. If suppression is partly internalized, workers carry the constraint's discipline with them even after exit; reclassification would show higher effective suppression than the measured 0.35. This affects the long-term stability prediction.
omegas.description: Extent to which suppression is structural or internalized in technologists' self-discipline.

network.dual_formulation_note: This constraint is one reading of the contested kernel 'human dignity in AI governance.' All four sibling readings (magisterial_integralist, secular_humanist, techno_optimist, pluralist_pragmatic) are separate constraint stories with distinct ε values, beneficiary/victim structures, and authority claims. No single reading is 'correct' — the framework models the kernel contest itself as a constraint family where readings coexist and influence each other. The Magisterial reading's effectiveness constrains the others' scope (it narrows the legitimacy space for pure transhumanism and efficiency-maximization) and is reciprocally constrained by them (secular-humanist and techno-optimist readings offer exit paths and counter-authorities).
